title: Reading a Twentieth of a Pixel
timing: MEASURED: Kokoro audio durations, plan rescaled to the speech, voiced figures pinned to Whisper word times

beats.title: THE PUZZLE
beats.narration_text: To know a galaxy's speed to one kilometer per second, you have to find a line of light to within two thousandths of a nanometer. The pixel that catches that light can be more than twenty times wider. So how do you read a mark that is a twentieth of the ruler's smallest division?
beats.visual_intent: Frame one, unnarrated: the empty three-panel frame (MOVED | WIDE | COUNTED) and the row of detector pixels. A ruler mark '1 km/s = 0.0022 nm' is drawn against one pixel; the pixel is bracketed '0.05 nm = 23x wider (my pixel)'. Title card 'Reading a Twentieth of a Pixel' for the first 2 s. Corner tag 'my simulation' all film.

on_screen.text: three-panel frame: MOVED | WIDE | COUNTED (empty, from frame one)
title: Reading a Twentieth of a Pixel

beats.title: THE SETUP
beats.narration_text: I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. I didn't use a telescope. I built the measurement: one line of light, a row of pixels, and photons arriving one at a time, so I could count exactly what each photon buys.
beats.visual_intent: The pixel row alone. Name chip 'Tanmay Kulkarni · Humanitarians AI'. A faint H-alpha line shape appears and the first photon drops into a pixel.

on_screen.text: name chip: Tanmay Kulkarni - Humanitarians AI
first photon drops into a pixel

beats.title: THE SHIFT
beats.narration_text: First, what moves. In the lab, hydrogen-alpha sits at six hundred fifty-six point two eight nanometers. A galaxy shifts it by its speed divided by the speed of light, times that. Andromeda's light arrives about point six six nanometers off. That is thirteen of my pixels, easy to see. The hard part is the last kilometer per second.
beats.visual_intent: The line at its lab position with 'H-alpha 656.28 nm (air)' and its source line; the galaxy's line shifted by 0.66 nm, bracket across 13 pixels. MOVED panel fills '0.66 nm = 300 km/s'. Formula as text: 'shift = speed / speed of light x 656.28 nm'. Source line held >= 2 s.
beats.status: PUBLIC (656.28 nm: standard reference citing NIST ASD) + OUR OWN arithmetic

on_screen.text: label: Andromeda, seen from the Sun
shift = speed / speed of light x 656.28 nm

beats.title: THE LINE IS A SMEAR
beats.narration_text: A spectral line is not a spike. It is a smear, because the gas that makes it is hot and moving. I gave mine a width of a hundred kilometers per second. Each photon lands somewhere in that smear, one at a time, and I only see which pixel caught it. Never where inside the pixel.
beats.visual_intent: The line drawn as a smear, bracket 'width 100 km/s (my choice)'. Photons land one at a time, each lighting a whole pixel; a dotted 'never seen' tick inside the pixel. WIDE panel fills '100 km/s'.

beats.title: TEN PHOTONS
beats.narration_text: Ten photons. My best guess for the center jumps around from run to run, off by about fifteen kilometers per second. That is most of a pixel. Ten photons say almost nothing.
beats.visual_intent: Ten photons. The best-guess marker and its error bar (about 15 km/s) beside the pixel bracket (23 km/s): the bar covers most of the pixel. COUNTED panel starts '10'.

on_screen.text: error bar: 14.6 km/s vs pixel 22.8 km/s
overlay: error covers 64% of one pixel

beats.title: A HUNDRED, A THOUSAND
beats.narration_text: A hundred photons, and I am off by four point six. A thousand, and I am off by one point four. A thousand photons, and my guess is good to six percent of a pixel. The pixel never got smaller. The guess got finer, because every photon is a small vote, and votes average.
beats.visual_intent: Three bars side by side, held together: 10 photons 14.6 km/s, 100 photons 4.6 km/s, 1,000 photons 1.4 km/s, each with the pixel bracket for scale. '1,000: 6% of one pixel'. Closing line on screen: the pixel never shrank.

on_screen.text: votes: each photon a small vote, averaged

beats.title: THE RULE
beats.narration_text: Here is the rule, and it is short. Three numbers matter. How far the line moved is the thing you want. How wide it is, and how many photons you caught, decide how well you know it. The error is the width of the line, divided by the square root of the photons. A hundred times the light buys ten times the precision. I checked it from ten photons up to a hundred thousand. It held to within about eight percent, the small cost of sorting photons into pixels.
beats.visual_intent: The three-panel frame, filled, then lit one panel at a time: MOVED (what you want), WIDE and COUNTED (decide how well you know it). The rule 'error = width / sqrt(photons)'. Plot: our measured errors against the rule, 10 to 100,000 photons, ratio 1.06 to 1.09. '100x the light = 10x the precision'.

on_screen.text: panels lit in turn: MOVED, WIDE, COUNTED
plot: measured vs rule, 10 to 100,000 photons

beats.title: THE PRICE LIST
beats.narration_text: So here is the price list. Each tenfold gain in precision costs a hundredfold more light. Four point six kilometers per second at a hundred photons. Point four six at ten thousand. Point one four at a hundred thousand. Precision is not free. You pay for it in light.
beats.visual_intent: A table, kept on screen: 100 photons 4.6 km/s; 10,000 photons 0.46 km/s; 100,000 photons 0.14 km/s; arrows 'x100 light = x10 precision'.

on_screen.text: x100 light = x10 precision; x10 light = x3.2

beats.title: WHOSE SPEED
beats.narration_text: One more thing the shift carries: us. A shift is relative, so it includes our own motion. Measured from the Sun, Andromeda's light reads about three hundred kilometers per second toward us. Take out the Sun's own motion, and the approach is about one hundred nine. Most of that three hundred is us.
beats.visual_intent: Two frames side by side, held >= 2 s: 'Seen from the Sun: about -300 km/s' and 'Galactic frame: -109 km/s', with the 192 km/s difference labelled 'Sun's own motion along the line of sight'. Source lines on screen: McConnachie 2012 (-300 +/- 4); van der Marel and Guhathakurta 2008 (-301); van der Marel et al. 2012 (-109.3 +/- 4.4).
beats.status: PUBLIC (three papers, FACTCHECK) + OUR OWN subtraction

beats.title: THE EDGE OF A GALAXY
beats.narration_text: Now zoom out to a spinning galaxy. Each point along the disk is its own measurement, with its own photons. The bright middle has plenty. The faint edge has few. In a toy disk I drew, the bars at the edge came out ten times longer than at the center. A rotation curve is not one line. It is a row of measurements, each with its own photon budget.
beats.visual_intent: A spinning disk (dots orbit each ring at the same speed, a flat curve) with rings and a rotation-curve plot; error bars grow outward (0.17 km/s at 1 kpc to 1.77 km/s at 15 kpc). Label held all beat: 'toy disk: assumed (exponential, scale length 3 kpc, 100,000 photons at center). Not a measured galaxy.' Edge bar '10x the center's'.

on_screen.text: label: toy disk, assumed. Not a measured galaxy.
bar at 15 kpc: 1.77 km/s = 10x the center's
sweep: a row of measurements, each its own photon budget

beats.title: THE BOUNDARY
beats.narration_text: What this does not cover. I tested one thing real spectra have, sky glow. Add ten times as many glow photons as line photons, and my error at a thousand photons went from one point four to three point four. I did not test blended neighbors or calibration error, and I measured nothing on a telescope. These are my simulated photons, and the rule they obeyed, bent by the glow.
beats.visual_intent: Two bars side by side, held >= 2 s: 'clean line: 1.4 km/s' and 'with 10x glow photons: 3.4 km/s'. Below, a three-row ledger: sky glow TESTED; blended neighbors NOT TESTED; calibration error NOT TESTED; telescope data NONE.

on_screen.text: ledger: blended neighbors, calibration NOT TESTED
arrow: error more than doubled by the glow

beats.title: YOUR TURN
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take a line a hundred kilometers per second wide. You want the speed to five. How many photons? The line's spread is about forty-two. Divide by five, then square it. About seventy-two, and closer to eighty-five once pixels get involved. Whenever you see a speed quoted that finely, ask how many photons paid for it.
beats.visual_intent: Exercise card: width 100 km/s, sigma 42.5 km/s, target 5 km/s; 'N = (42.5 / 5)^2 = 72'; then '85 in my simulation (pixels)'. Final 3 s: the film's title card.
beats.status: MEAS (sim at 72 and 85 photons) + the formula
